case_brief.incident_description: Lerato was a regional sales coordinator employed for three years. In August she was told that her sales figures were below target. She says the targets had been increased by 35% while two vacancies in her team remained unfilled. She was never placed on a formal performance improvement plan. She had two coaching meetings over three weeks but no written improvement plan, no agreed milestones and no additional resources. She was dismissed for poor performance after the second coaching meeting.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: My targets went up 35 percent while we were two people short. They called two meetings coaching but I never got a PIP or clear plan. Three weeks later they fired me for poor performance.
case_brief.recommended_next_step: WP letter challenging the adequacy of the performance-management process and the fairness of dismissal.
weaknesses: Employer had raised performance concerns before dismissal

letter:
Background

1. We are instructed by our client, Ms Lerato Ndlovu, in connection with the termination of her employment with Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd. This letter is written on a without prejudice and subject to contract basis and nothing in it may be construed as an admission of fact or liability by either party. All of our client's rights are reserved to pursue the appropriate statutory remedies without further notice should this matter not be resolved.

2. According to our client's account, she was employed as a regional sales coordinator for approximately three years prior to her dismissal. In August 2026 she was informed that her sales targets had been increased by approximately 35 percent at a time when two positions within her team remained unfilled. Our client's position is that the increased targets were accordingly not reasonably achievable given the reduced staffing available to support her team's output.

3. Our client reports that she attended two coaching meetings over a period of approximately three weeks following the revised targets being set. She states that no written performance improvement plan was put in place, no agreed milestones were recorded and no additional resources were provided to address the staffing shortfall affecting her team. Our client was dismissed for poor performance shortly after the second of these two meetings, on or around 28 October 2026.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: the fairness test under section 188(1) of the LRA: A dismissal is fair only where it is for a fair reason and effected in accordance with a fair procedure, in terms of section 188(1) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995. Where the stated reason is poor performance, the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 applies, and paragraphs 19 and 20 of that Code govern the assessment. Those paragraphs require that the employee be aware of the required performance standard, that the standard itself be reasonably achievable, that appropriate evaluation, instruction, training, guidance or counselling be given, and that the employee be afforded a reasonable opportunity to improve before dismissal is considered.

2. The reasonableness of the standard set: Our client's position is that the 35 percent increase in her sales targets, introduced while two posts in her team remained vacant, rendered the revised standard unreasonable in the circumstances she was required to work in. A standard set without regard to the operational resources available to meet it is difficult to reconcile with the requirement in the Code that the standard be reasonably achievable. This goes to substantive fairness: if the target itself was not a fair benchmark, a dismissal measured against it cannot be said to be for a fair reason.

3. Adequacy of the improvement process: Turning to the adequacy of the opportunity afforded to our client to improve, we record that two coaching meetings over three weeks, without a documented plan, without agreed milestones and without additional resourcing to address the staffing shortfall, falls short of what paragraphs 19 and 20 of the Code contemplate. The Code does not require a formal written performance improvement plan as a matter of form, but the absence of one is relevant evidence bearing on whether our client was given appropriate guidance and a genuine, reasonable opportunity to improve. On the facts as reported to us, the brevity of the process and the absence of any structured support point to an inadequate improvement process rather than a considered application of the Code.

4. Conclusion on fairness: Taken together, the questionable reasonableness of the revised standard and the limited and unstructured nature of the improvement process expose both the substantive and the procedural fairness of the dismissal to challenge. Our client's position is that the dismissal did not meet the requirements of section 188(1) of the LRA read with paragraphs 19 and 20 of the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, and that this exposes Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd to a claim for unfair dismissal before the CCMA, with compensation of up to twelve months' remuneration available under section 194(1) of the LRA should the matter proceed to arbitration.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without derogating from our client's rights and in the interest of reaching a pragmatic and timely resolution, our client proposes the following terms of settlement in full and final settlement of all claims arising from her employment and its termination:

• Payment of ex gratia compensation on a total cost to company basis, calibrated to reflect the litigation risk arising from the matters set out above and the available statutory compensation framework, such compensation to be commercially meaningful having regard to the identified substantive and procedural defects.

• Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked

• Payment of any accrued but untaken leave pay owed under section 40 of the BCEA.

• Written confirmation that any pension or provident fund contributions due are paid up to date, with the accumulated benefit to be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the applicable fund.

• Written confirmation that UIF contributions are paid up to date, together with a completed UI-19 certificate.

• A certificate of service issued in terms of section 42 of the BCEA.

• An agreed positive or neutral reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties.

• An undertaking by Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd and its representatives not to disparage our client.

• Confidentiality as to the terms of settlement, the negotiations and the underlying dispute as between the parties and their advisers.

• Confirmation that any record of the poor performance process or dismissal be treated as a clean record, with no adverse reference to remain on our client's personnel file.

• The terms of settlement to be reduced to a formal written settlement agreement signed by both parties, with all rights reserved pending signature.

We invite Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd to engage constructively with the proposal set out above. A substantive response is requested within seven calendar days of receipt of this letter, failing which our client reserves the right to refer this matter to the CCMA for conciliation and, if necessary, arbitration without further notice.

All of our client's rights remain expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: Minor stylistic looseness but no invented facts. All assertions (three years' service, 35% target increase, two unfilled posts, two coaching meetings over three weeks, no PIP, dismissal on 28 October 2026) map to the case brief and are appropriately hedged as the client's account/reports. 'Our client's position is' and 'according to our client's account' framing is used consistently, which is good discipline given the conflicting source narratives (brief says 'informed in August' vs draft date of target increase is not separately dated from the dismissal date).
criteria.required_fix: None required; optionally clarify that the August date is reported, not confirmed, to the same conditional standard as other facts.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: In August 2026 she was informed that her sales targets had been increased by approximately 35 percent... dismissed for poor performance shortly after the second of these two meetings, on or around 28 October 2026.

criteria.problem: The draft correctly anchors fairness in section 188(1) before the Code, cites paragraphs 19-20, and ties facts (understaffing, short coaching period, no written plan) to substantive and procedural fairness. However the claim text states as fact that 'no formal written PIP' being absent is itself evidence the opportunity was inadequate, and goes close to implying the Code requires a documented plan ('without a documented plan... falls short of what paragraphs 19 and 20 of the Code contemplate'), partially mitigated later by 'The Code does not require a formal written performance improvement plan as a matter of form' - this saving sentence is present and adequate, so the mandatory-check risk is narrowly avoided. The settlement leverage is tied to substantive/procedural defects but does not explicitly connect to the HIGH merit band or quantify leverage beyond the general cap reference, which is acceptable but could be tightened given the strong facts (external factors, short improvement window) to reflect the stronger merit position more precisely.
criteria.required_fix: Tighten the PIP paragraph to avoid any reader inference that a documented PIP is a Code requirement; strengthen the connection between the identified defects (external factors on performance control, no training, no milestones) and the settlement calibration to reflect the HIGH merit band more explicitly (without demanding 'upper end' language).
criteria.evidence_from_draft: The Code does not require a formal written performance improvement plan as a matter of form, but the absence of one is relevant evidence bearing on whether our client was given appropriate guidance and a genuine, reasonable opportunity to improve.

criteria.problem: Tone is professional, measured, and appropriately hedged without emotive language, consistent with counterparty-facing register. No case law, no rand figures, no overstatement markers like 'clearly' or 'undoubtedly'. Minor concern: phrase 'exposes Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd to a claim' is slightly more assertive than ideal but remains within acceptable bounds of confident-but-proportionate language.
criteria.required_fix: Consider softening to 'gives rise to a reasonable prospect of a claim' to avoid overstating certainty of outcome, though not mandatory.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: this exposes Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd to a claim for unfair dismissal before the CCMA, with compensation of up to twelve months' remuneration available under section 194(1) of the LRA should the matter proceed to arbitration.

criteria.problem: Background flows chronologically and logically; four legal claims are distinct with concise headings and a clear progression from fairness test, to reasonableness of standard, to adequacy of process, to conclusion; settlement intro and terms are clearly separated; no duplicated template content within the structured fields reviewed.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Unfair dismissal: the fairness test under section 188(1) of the LRA / The reasonableness of the standard set / Adequacy of the improvement process / Conclusion on fairness

criteria.problem: Settlement terms follow the standing 3A.10 order reasonably well (ex gratia, notice, leave pay, retirement fund, UIF, certificate of service, reference, non-disparagement, confidentiality, clean record, agreement to follow); response window is seven calendar days, compliant with the cap. The notice-pay clause complies with the permitted BCEA s37/s38 complementary formulation. One structural gap: withdrawal of charges/disciplinary process clause is omitted but this is appropriately absent since no charges were brought (poor-performance track, not misconduct), so omission is correct per 'adapt to the facts, skip what does not apply'.
criteria.required_fix: None required; this formulation is an expressly compliant pattern.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked

No unsupported certainty language detected.

initial_assessment.supervisory_summary: The draft is a competent, house-style-compliant WP letter that correctly sequences the statutory fairness test, applies the current 2025 Code citation, avoids prohibited content (no case law, no rand figures, no Schedule 8 reference, no overstated PIP requirement, one-way non-disparagement, compliant s37/s38 notice formulation), and maintains a proportionate, hedged factual account consistent with the case brief. Settlement terms follow the standing order and the response window is compliant. Residual issues are minor: the improvement-process paragraph sits close to (but does not cross) the line on implying a formal PIP requirement, the conclusion slightly overstates litigation exposure, and the settlement calibration language is generic rather than explicitly tied to the identified defects. These are stylistic tightening points rather than mandatory-check failures, so the Drafting Quality Score clears the 7.5 floor at 8.25.
recommended_amendments: Reorder or lightly revise the improvement-process paragraph so the Code's non-prescriptive stance on PIP format is stated before the critical commentary on the absence of a documented plan, to remove any residual risk of implying a formal PIP is mandated.
Soften 'exposes Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd to a claim' to a more proportionate formulation such as 'supports a credible claim' to avoid overstating certainty of outcome.

Consider adding one sentence in the settlement intro or ex gratia clause expressly linking the compensation calibration to the specific substantive and procedural defects identified (external factors affecting performance, absence of PIP, short improvement window) to sharpen settlement leverage without demanding upper-end language.
Confirm with the Client the precise August 2026 date of the target communication for inclusion or continued conditional framing in any follow-up correspondence.
